Why do South Asians get type 2 diabetes at much lower body weights? The answer is in their fat cells.

These are fat cells from two young men with the same BMI. The South Asian man's are on the left. The white man's are on the right.

At the same BMI as white Europeans, South Asians carry more body fat, bigger fat cells, more liver fat, and higher insulin. Here is what the studies show.

1. Same BMI, much bigger fat cells.
In 29 South Asian and 18 white men, average age 27, BMI was 24 vs 23. Body fat was 22% vs 15%. The average belly fat cell was 3,491 vs 1,648 µm² in cross section. Treating the cells as spheres, that is about 3 times the volume of fat per cell on average. The samples in the image show an even larger difference. The larger the fat cells, the worse the insulin resistance. Visceral fat was the same in both groups.

2. Matched for age and BMI, still more insulin.
Asian Indians matched to white adults had similar fasting glucose but higher fasting insulin, and they cleared glucose about 40% less well on a clamp test (4.7 vs 7.5 mg/kg/min).

3. Fat cell size explains much of the insulin gap.
After adjusting for age, sex and BMI, South Asians had larger fat cells, liver fat of 9.9% vs 2.5%, and higher fasting insulin. Adjusting for fat cell size cut the insulin difference in half.

4. Lean and young.
Among 482 lean young adults, insulin resistance was 2 to 3 times more common in Asian Indians than in any other group. The men had about twice the liver fat of white men.

5. It starts in childhood.
South Asian children aged 8 to 11 in Britain were not heavier than white children, but their fasting insulin was 53% higher, with similar blood glucose.

My view: fat cells can only store so much. When they are full, they become insulin resistant and release more fat into the blood, and that fat ends up in the liver and muscle. Insulin rises to compensate. South Asians appear to reach that limit at a lower body weight.

For a South Asian person, a normal BMI does not mean normal metabolism. Fasting insulin, waist size and liver fat say more than weight.

hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
Infrared vs. traditional sauna. Are the benefits really the same?

I get asked this question constantly! My take is that infrared saunas can absolutely produce meaningful heat stress, but they're not necessarily equivalent to traditional Finnish saunas.

Traditional saunas heat the surrounding air, typically around 175-195°F, whereas infrared saunas use radiant heat and generally operate at lower temperatures (110-150°F).

The important question is how much thermal stress you're actually generating.

I personally prefer traditional Finnish saunas. Most of the compelling long-term evidence linking sauna use to lower cardiovascular mortality and dementia risk comes from traditional Finnish sauna studies.

But if infrared is what you have access to, I wouldn't dismiss it!

My recommendation would be to fully preheat the sauna and recognize that you may need a longer exposure to generate comparable heat stress. Importantly, there's no established temperature-duration formula that makes infrared equivalent to traditional sauna.

Infrared saunas can deliver substantial heat stress, but whether they produce the same long-term health benefits as traditional saunas remains an open question.

On the other hand, there is a growing body of evidence that IR saunas, as part of a clinical hyperthermia protocol, can have substantial antidepressant effects in people with major depressive disorder! 

At the end of the day, it seems deliberate heat exposure (up to a point) is broadly beneficial however we get there.
hits.draft_en:
Rhonda Patrick on infrared versus normal saunas. Infrared can give you real heat stress, but it runs cooler, roughly 43 to 65°C against about 80 to 90°C for a traditional Finnish sauna. Most of the strong long-term evidence on heart health and dementia comes from the traditional kind.

Her advice if infrared is what you've got: preheat it properly and expect to stay in a bit longer. Nobody knows yet if the long-term benefits match.

So don't fuss over the type. Use what you can get to, use it regularly, drink water, and talk to your GP first if your heart isn't right.

Aging is a multi-scale physiological process that we can’t actually measure directly. Biomarkers are like the blind men touching the elephant; able to know a piece, but never the whole.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
Hibernating brown bears have roughly double the cholesterol and triglycerides of healthy humans—yet show no atherosclerosis or heart disease. 
During winter hibernation, free-ranging brown bears (Ursus arctos) experience plasma cholesterol levels around 12 mmol/L (versus ~5 mmol/L in humans) and elevated triglycerides, along with obesity, physical inactivity for months, and other metabolic stressors that would typically promote vascular disease in humans. 
Histopathology of coronary arteries and aortic arches from adult bears has repeatedly shown no fatty streaks, foam cell infiltration, inflammation, or atherosclerotic lesions—even in animals that have lived through multiple hibernation cycles. 
Key protective mechanisms identified in research include:
•  LDL particles that are larger and have 5–10× lower affinity for arterial proteoglycans (the binding that helps drive plaque formation in humans)
•  Higher plasma cholesterol efflux capacity
•  Stabilized or more cardioprotective HDL composition (including increased HDL2b)
•  Greater antioxidant capacity and reduced inflammatory/oxidative markers during hibernation
These findings come from multiple studies on Scandinavian brown bears, including work in Scientific Reports, the Journal of Lipid Research, and related papers. 
The takeaway is straightforward: high circulating cholesterol and triglycerides do not automatically produce atherosclerosis. Context—lipoprotein structure, function, inflammatory status, and overall metabolic handling—matters. Bears offer a natural model of high lipids without the expected vascular damage.

In 1982 Barry Brenner published a paper in the New England Journal of Medicine.
He proposed that a high-protein diet raised pressure inside the glomerulus, forced the kidney to filter more, and, over time, wore the tissue out. The idea came from animal work in which nephrons had already been reduced. The remaining units overworked. Protein restriction slowed the damage in those models. The paper was widely cited. Protein restriction entered advice for people with kidney disease and, by extension, for anyone who ate a lot of meat.
Later work examined the claim in people whose kidneys were intact. Meta-analyses of trials found that higher protein raised the measured filtration rate, as expected, but did not produce progressive loss of function. Changes in creatinine and other markers of injury did not differ between high- and moderate-protein groups. Observational data in healthy adults likewise failed to show that protein intake predicted later kidney disease. The filtration increase appeared to be an adaptation, not a step toward failure.
The original hypothesis held for kidneys that were already reduced. It did not hold for kidneys that were not. The distinction took decades to settle in the literature. The advice for healthy people did not.

Steve Irwin was one of the most passionate animal lovers on the planet. He also wasn’t a vegetarian, and he had a clear reason why.
In a 2001 interview with Scientific American he explained that he went through a phase where he seriously considered going vegetarian. He researched it hard. His conclusion was the opposite of what most people assume.

He used a simple land-use example: one cow could keep him fed for roughly a month. That same piece of land could still have trees, grass, kangaroos, wallabies, goannas, birds, and the rest of the Australian wildlife living in and around it. The cow and the wild animals could coexist.

A plant-only diet for the same period, he argued, required clearing more land just for crops. Once you level that ground for rice or whatever else, almost nothing else can live there except a few pest insects. Habitat gone. Wildlife gone.

He wasn’t anti-meat. He was anti-destroying habitat. And he drew a hard line on which animals should be eaten. He hated the idea of farming or eating Australia’s icons — kangaroos, emus, crocodiles. Those animals were part of the country’s identity and tourism. He wanted people eating the livestock that already occupied grazing land (beef, lamb, etc.), not turning the bush into more monoculture or harvesting the wildlife itself.

On the day he died he had a classic Aussie breakfast: bacon and eggs. He lived a high-output outdoor life and fueled it with real food, not ideology.

Irwin’s position was straightforward: protect the wild animals, keep the land working, and don’t pretend that clearing more ground for plants is automatically better for nature. A lot of modern “eat less meat for the environment” arguments still haven’t grappled with the trade-off he laid out more than 20 years ago.
hits.draft_en:

The brain is not locked to sugar. It is a hybrid that prefers ketones once they are available. Cahill showed it sixty years ago in men who were not supposed to stay clear-headed. They did.

Briana Pobiner spent months trailing lions in Kenya to answer a simple question: after a kill, is there still enough meat left for someone else?
Critics of the passive scavenging idea had argued that lions finish their prey so thoroughly that early hominids would have found only scraps—barely worth the risk or the walk. Pobiner waited until the cats were done, then recorded what remained on the bones. She worked in a lion-dominated savanna with relatively low hyena competition, closer to the conditions some models propose for early East African habitats.
On larger kills (zebra- and wildebeest-sized), 95 percent of the bones still carried at least some edible flesh. Half of them retained bulk muscle—more than 10 percent of the original mass. Even a “defleshed” zebra carcass could still yield roughly 30-plus pounds of meat, enough to meet the daily caloric needs of an adult Homo erectus several times over. Smaller prey left far less. 
Lions do not consume every last ounce of muscle before they move on, especially on bigger animals. The leftovers are not negligible. Combined with marrow and brain, which felids leave largely untouched, a single abandoned kill could have supplied a meaningful amount of high-quality animal food without requiring a full hunt.
This does not prove early hominids only scavenged. It does show that waiting for lions to finish was not an empty strategy. In the right habitats and seasons, the meat was still there.

John Yudkin (1910–1995) was a British physiologist and the founding Professor of Nutrition at Queen Elizabeth College, London. He is best known for his 1972 book Pure, White and Deadly (originally Sweet and Dangerous in the US), which argued that rising sugar (sucrose) consumption—not saturated fat—was a major driver of obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, dental caries, and other conditions. 
He had been making the case since at least 1957 based on epidemiological data and experiments. He noted that sugar intake correlated more strongly with coronary mortality than fat intake in many comparisons, and that patients with atherosclerotic disease consumed more sucrose. He also observed that sugar was a relatively recent dietary addition (becoming widespread only in the last few centuries), while animal fats had been a staple far longer. He wrote that there is no physiological requirement for sugar and that “if only a small fraction of what we already know about the effects of sugar were to be revealed in relation to any other material used as a food additive, that material would promptly be banned.” 
The book and its author faced strong pushback from the sugar industry, processed-food manufacturers, and advocates of the saturated-fat hypothesis (notably Ancel Keys). Funding and publication faced interference, and his reputation suffered; he died in 1995 largely overlooked by the mainstream of his era. Later work on fructose metabolism, insulin resistance, and the outcomes of the low-fat era has led many to view his warnings as prophetic. The book was reissued in later editions with an introduction by Robert Lustig.

The so-called “Indian Enigma” is one of the more awkward facts in global nutrition. For years India has posted higher rates of child stunting than large parts of Sub-Saharan Africa, even though India’s GDP per capita has been meaningfully higher and its average calorie intake has not been lower. 

The gap was never subtle. Researchers kept documenting it and then mostly looked the other way when the most obvious dietary difference came up.

India’s public diet, especially among the groups that drive the national average, is built on rice, wheat, and other cheap cereals. Animal foods—meat, eggs, dairy, fish—are consumed in low quantities by a large share of the population. 

Sub-Saharan African diets, even in very poor countries, have historically included more meat, milk, eggs, and small fish. Not high amounts by Western standards, but enough to supply the amino acids, bioavailable iron, zinc, and other nutrients that cereal staples simply do not deliver in useful form. Height is not built on starch alone.

The usual explanations get rolled out—open defecation, infections, maternal height, caste disparities. Some of those factors are real. None of them erase the dietary pattern. When you compare upper-caste Indian children (still largely vegetarian or low-animal-food) with African averages, the stunting gap shrinks but does not disappear in the direction people expect. 

Recent data show India has improved to roughly 29%, putting it near the Sub-Saharan average. Several poorer African countries that never adopted a rice-and-wheat-plus-lentils model still sit lower.

This is not a mystery that requires advanced modeling. Stunting tracks chronic deficits in high-quality protein and micronutrients during the first 1,000 days. Cereals are cheap and filling. They are poor raw material for building children. 

Countries that kept more animal foods in the diet, even under worse economic conditions, produced taller kids on average. The Indian data have shown this for decades. Most official commentary still prefers to talk about everything except the missing meat, eggs, and milk.

Steller’s sea cow was a 30-foot, roughly 10-ton sirenian that lived in the cold, shallow coastal waters of the Commander Islands. Georg Steller documented it in 1741 after Bering’s expedition was shipwrecked there. Within 27 years it was gone.

Russian fur traders and sailors hunted it hard. Contemporary accounts describe the meat as tasting like the best beef and the fat as equal to the finest butter. One animal could provision an entire crew for weeks. These were slow-moving, nearshore animals with no real fear of people, thick blubber, and low reproductive rates. Easy targets that delivered an enormous return in high-quality animal food.

That is the pattern Baz Edmeades traces in Megafauna. Large animals with slow life histories were repeatedly taken out by humans once they became accessible. The sea cow is a late, well-documented example: a coastal giant whose primary value was dense meat and fat. Hunters did not invent a new preference when they killed it. They acted on the same preference that has driven humans toward large game for a very long time.

Modern accounts sometimes frame these extinctions as pure tragedy or ecological mistake. The primary sources are clearer. The people who encountered the animals repeatedly noted how good the meat and fat were and how efficiently one kill fed many people. That does not erase the outcome. It does explain the incentive.

Giant tortoises spent millions of years perfecting one defense: a shell that stopped lions.
Baz Edmeades argues in Megafauna that this same shell became irrelevant the moment tool-using hominins arrived. A large rock or a sharp stone edge could open what claws and teeth could not. The animals were slow, non-aggressive, and carried substantial meat in a package that did not run away. Once the method was figured out, 200-year-old tortoises turned into low-effort, high-yield food.
Giant tortoises had lived on the African mainland for a long time. They disappeared near the beginning of the Pleistocene, roughly two million years ago—well before the later wave of mammalian megafauna extinctions and before the rise of Homo sapiens. Edmeades sees the timing as more than coincidence. The innovation of using stones as tools and weapons gave early hominins access to a resource that had previously been effectively protected by its armor. Evolution had no time to respond.
The same pattern repeated elsewhere. On islands reached later by modern humans, endemic giant tortoises were among the first large animals to vanish. Slow reproduction, no fear of new predators, and the ability to be stored alive made them especially vulnerable once people arrived with the capacity to break shells.
Edmeades treats the tortoise story as an early illustration of a larger shift. Before hominins, defenses improved at the speed of natural selection. After tool use, a single behavioral innovation could neutralize an ancient adaptation overnight. The shell that had worked against every previous predator failed against a primate that could pick up a rock.
The result was reliable animal food with minimal risk—an early, low-skill route to meat that required neither speed nor the ability to take down large mammals.

Abetalipoproteinemia produces some of the lowest LDL cholesterol levels possible in humans—essentially undetectable—because the body cannot assemble apoB-containing lipoproteins at all. 

On paper that looks like the ultimate “low LDL” success story. In reality it is a severe disease.

The same genetic defect (MTTP mutations) that abolishes LDL also abolishes the ability to absorb dietary fat and the fat-soluble vitamins that travel with it. Infants present with steatorrhea, diarrhea, and failure to thrive. Without massive vitamin replacement, especially vitamin E at 100–300 IU/kg/day, patients develop progressive ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, spinocerebellar degeneration, and retinitis pigmentosa. Vitamin A deficiency adds night blindness and further retinal damage; vitamin K deficiency produces bleeding tendencies. Red cells become acanthocytes. Even with treatment the transport system remains broken, so tissue vitamin E stays low and a strict low-fat diet is required for life.

Very low LDL here is not a protective biomarker. It is a marker of a broken fat-transport system whose downstream effects are neurological and retinal damage driven by vitamin E (and other fat-soluble nutrient) deficiency. The condition illustrates that human physiology is built around the absorption and utilization of dietary fats and the vitamins they carry. When that machinery fails, the consequences are severe—regardless of how low the LDL number reads on a lab report.

OpenAI models helped researchers—operating as part of our Patch the Planet initiative—discover critical security flaws in PHP, an open-source programming language used to run an estimated 70% of websites.
